title: Has the Chinese yuan's rise in global usage hit a wall?
gist: The yuan's post-Ukraine internationalization surge stalled and partly reversed after mid-2024: its SWIFT payment share fell from a 4.7% July 2024 peak to 2.75% (sixth place, behind the Canadian dollar) and Hong Kong CHATS RMB volumes plunged, while only China's own CIPS rail hit all-time highs. Migration of payments off SWIFT onto CIPS explains only about one-fifth of the CHATS decline, so the retreat is largely real, and the dollar's share of global FX transactions actually rose from 87% to 89%. The conclusion drawn is that yuan internationalization now functions as a sanctions insurance policy rather than a live challenge to the dollar.

insights.claim: The Chinese yuan's share of global payments on the SWIFT network peaked at 4.7 percent in July 2024 and has since fallen back to 2.75 percent, making it only the world's sixth most used payments currency, behind even the Canadian dollar.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: The 'de-dollarization via RMB' trade has no confirming payments data; monitor monthly SWIFT RMB Tracker prints before pricing yuan reserve-currency optionality.
insights.quote: It peaked at 4.7 percent of global payments by July 2024, passing the Japanese yen and Canadian dollar to become the fourth most used.

insights.claim: Headlines claiming China is 'ditching' the dollar or that the yuan is 'taking over the dollar's role' are contradicted by the data: yuan international use has decreased over the last two years both in absolute terms and as a share of global payments.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: A widely held consensus narrative is empirically wrong right now — fade de-dollarization headlines that cite yuan payment adoption as evidence.
insights.quote: is that the yuan's momentum has faded. By some important measures its international use has even decreased, both in absolute terms and as a share of global payments over the last two years.

insights.claim: Chained SWIFT month-on-month volume data show renminbi volumes on SWIFT declined 24 percent from the July 2024 peak as of January 2026, disproving the argument that the yuan's falling share merely reflects faster growth in other currencies.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: The decline is in absolute volume, not just relative share — a stronger negative signal for yuan-linked settlement infrastructure and offshore RMB liquidity.
insights.quote: Chaining together SWIFT data on month-on-month volume changes shows RMB volumes on SWIFT declined relative to the July 2024 peak by 24 percent as of January 2026.

insights.claim: The yuan's 2023-24 surge in global usage was driven by geopolitical tailwinds — sanctions on Russia after its invasion of Ukraine and the reordering of Russian trade — rather than by structural demand, which explains why it faded once that one-off reallocation was absorbed.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: Treat sanction-driven currency share gains as one-time level shifts, not trend breaks; the next leg requires a new sanctions shock, not organic adoption.

insights.claim: Renminbi internationalization proceeds in waves and can reverse: the yuan share of SWIFT payments rose from under 1 percent in 2010 to 2.8 percent by late 2015, then fell back and stagnated around 2 percent for five years after a sharp depreciation and tightened capital controls.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: Use the 2015-16 episode as the base-rate template: a depreciation plus capital-control tightening is the trigger that historically kills yuan usage momentum.

themes.theme: CIPS vs CHATS vs SWIFT divergence

insights.claim: China's Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) is registering all-time high yuan volumes while Hong Kong's CHATS system and the yuan's SWIFT share remain far below their mid-2024 peaks — the first time these metrics have diverged.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: Track CIPS volume separately from SWIFT share — the two are no longer substitutable proxies for yuan internationalization, and conflating them produces wrong conclusions in either direction.
insights.quote: All have come up from late 2025 lows, but CIPS is registering all-time highs while CHATS and SWIFT remain far below the peak.
insights.locator: Since the mid-2024 peak, however, the overall trend

insights.claim: Migration of payments from Hong Kong's CHATS onto CIPS can explain only about one-fifth of the observed decline: CHATS average daily RMB volume fell by over 1 trillion yuan between June 2024 and June 2026 while CIPS volume rose only about 200 billion yuan.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: The measurement-artifact defense of yuan adoption fails an arithmetic test — the decline in offshore yuan clearing is mostly real, which matters for Hong Kong's role as the offshore RMB hub.
insights.quote: CHATS average daily RMB volume has fallen by over 1 trillion yuan from June 2024 to June 2026, while CIPS volume is only up by one-fifth of that, about 200 billion yuan.
insights.locator: Some of the yuan's decline n CHATS may be due to migration

insights.claim: CIPS's network of direct participants — banks that can settle end-to-end without ever sending a SWIFT message — grew from 79 banks in January 2023 to 210 today, mechanically removing yuan volume from SWIFT-based statistics.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: SWIFT-derived currency shares will structurally understate the yuan over time; the direct-participant count is the cleanest leading indicator of how much data goes dark.
insights.quote: This network(link is external) of direct participants has grown rapidly from 79 banks since January 2023 to 210 today.
insights.locator: CIPS, however, also has its own independent messaging system

insights.claim: Hong Kong's CHATS handles three times as many payments as CIPS, so the plunge in CHATS yuan volume since mid-2024 is the more consequential data point for gauging real offshore yuan usage.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: Analysts anchoring on CIPS headlines are watching the smaller pipe; CHATS RMB volume is the higher-signal series for offshore RMB demand.
insights.locator: The data paint a mixed picture

insights.claim: Both CIPS and CHATS yuan volumes more than doubled from mid-2022 to mid-2024 — CIPS from around 350 billion to 770 billion yuan and CHATS from 1.5 trillion to 3.3 trillion yuan — establishing how much of the subsequent move is round-trip.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: Gives concrete levels to benchmark future prints against, rather than relying on percentage-share optics.
insights.locator: Figure 2 shows the payment volume in billions of yuan

insights.claim: The crisis in the Strait of Hormuz appears to have revived CIPS growth, indicating that geopolitical disruption events, not commercial adoption, are the reliable trigger for step-changes in yuan payment rails.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: Treat CIPS volume as a geopolitical stress gauge — spikes there flag sanction-avoidance or energy-trade rerouting rather than yuan strength.
insights.locator: China's Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) is the main bright spot

insights.claim: The US dollar remains at historic highs in global foreign exchange payments and its share of BIS-measured global FX transactions actually increased from 87 percent in 2013 to 89 percent by mid-June 2025, despite widespread sanctions concerns.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: Dollar-funding and dollar-clearing franchises face no measurable erosion; structural short-dollar theses built on reserve-status decay lack data support.
insights.quote: Despite all the concerns about sanctions, the dollar's share increased from 87 to 89 percent.
insights.locator: Looking globally, the Bank for International Settlements reports

insights.claim: The yuan's rise from 2 percent of global FX transactions in 2013 to 8.5 percent in mid-2025 came entirely at the expense of currencies other than the dollar, meaning the yuan has been displacing the euro, yen and other minors rather than the greenback.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: The competitive pressure from the yuan lands on second-tier reserve currencies, not on the dollar — relevant for EUR and JPY internationalization narratives rather than USD.
insights.quote: the yuan has increased from being on one side of 2 percent of global foreign exchange transactions in 2013 to 8.5 percent in mid-June 2025, but its rise has come entirely at the expense of currencies other than the dollar
insights.locator: Looking globally, the Bank for International Settlements reports

insights.claim: SAFE data show the US dollar has held a steady roughly 90 percent share of all Chinese cross-border payments not settled in yuan, proving China has not diversified into the euro or other alternatives when it moves away from yuan settlement.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: There is no third-currency hedge inside China's own payment mix — any yuan stall translates directly into continued dollar dependence.
insights.quote: The SAFE data also show the dollar has remained steady with around a 90 percent share of any payments not settled in yuan, suggesting China has not ditched dollar payments to transact in other currencies like the euro.
insights.locator: Another way to look at yuan payments is through the State Administration

insights.claim: The yuan's failure to gain share during a period of rising global concern about the dollar is itself the surprising result, implying Beijing will need entirely new growth drivers to close the gap with the greenback.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: If the yuan cannot gain when dollar sentiment is weak, the bar for future gains is higher — argues for structurally low probability of near-term reserve-currency rotation.
insights.quote: The lack of gains in a period with rising global concerns about the dollar is particularly surprising, and it suggests Beijing will need to find new growth drivers if it wants to close the gap with the greenback.
insights.locator: Conclusion

insights.claim: Yuan internationalization is better understood as an insurance policy — infrastructure held ready to be activated for large-scale payments if sanctions force China off the dollar — rather than as an active campaign that is currently winning share.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: Reframes CIPS capacity as tail-risk hedging capacity: its value shows up only in a US-China sanctions scenario, not in baseline flow data.
insights.quote: Yuan internationalization may be more of an insurance policy, ready to be activated for larger scale payments if sanctions force China off the dollar.
insights.locator: Conclusion

insights.claim: China is deliberately accepting divergence from global payment standards in exchange for resilience against future sanctions, as evidenced by yuan payments increasingly bypassing the SWIFT network entirely.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: Expect progressive loss of visibility into China-linked flows for Western compliance and macro analysts — a data-availability risk for anyone modeling China trade finance.
insights.quote: It is a sign that China is prioritizing resilience to potential future sanctions and self-sufficiency, even at the risk of diverging from global payment standards.
insights.locator: Nevertheless, CIPS's divergence from these other metrics

insights.claim: Chinese policymakers have failed to reconcile the capital-account openness a major global currency requires with the domestic stability they enforce through strict capital controls, which is the binding constraint on yuan internationalization.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: Watch capital-account liberalization steps as the only real leading indicator of a durable yuan regime change; payment-rail announcements are noise without it.
insights.quote: But Chinese policymakers have struggled to reconcile the openness that having a major global currency would require with domestic stability reinforced through strict capital controls.
insights.locator: Fits and starts for the yuan

insights.claim: PBOC governor Pan Gongsheng framed the case for the yuan in defensive terms in 2025, warning that a global dominant currency 'tends to be instrumentalized or weaponized' and praising efforts to weaken excessive reliance on a single sovereign currency.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: Official rhetoric confirms the motive is sanctions-proofing, not commercial competitiveness — sets expectations for policy that prioritizes control over convertibility.
insights.quote: a "global dominant currency tends to be instrumentalized or weaponized"
insights.locator: People's Bank of China governor Pan Gongsheng warned

insights.claim: Xi Jinping in 2023 explicitly called for China to become a 'strong financial country' with a currency having wide use in international trade, investment and FX markets and even status as a global reserve currency, making yuan internationalization a top-level political objective.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: Political priority means policy support persists through stalled data — expect further rail-building announcements regardless of adoption metrics.

insights.claim: 72 percent of China's goods trade is still settled in currencies other than the yuan, even after the yuan-settled share climbed from a 2017 low of 11 percent to 28 percent in the first half of 2025.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: Sets a concrete ceiling on the 'trade-settlement de-dollarization' story; roughly three-quarters of the world's largest goods exporter still invoices in foreign currency.
insights.quote: It is also a useful reminder that 72 percent of China's goods trade is still settled in other currencies.

insights.claim: China's yuan-settled share of goods trade fell from 23 percent in 2015 to 11 percent in 2017 before recovering to 28 percent, demonstrating that a decade of net progress amounted to only five percentage points and that reversals of over half the share are possible.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: Quantifies the downside case for yuan trade settlement — a repeat of 2015-17 would halve the current share, which matters for offshore RMB deposit and hedging demand.

insights.claim: SAFE data show the yuan reached roughly half of China's overall cross-border settlements by early 2023 largely at the dollar's expense, but has stagnated at that level since and stopped gaining, with yuan payment growth only keeping pace with continued demand for dollar settlement.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: Rising absolute yuan volumes are misleading — the share metric has been flat for over three years, so growth reflects trade volume, not currency substitution.

insights.claim: The composition of China's cross-border bank payments has shifted decisively toward finance: goods and services trade settlement fell from around three quarters of these payments before 2019 to roughly 47 percent today as financial transactions grew much faster.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: China's cross-border flows are now majority financial, making them more sentiment- and rate-sensitive and less anchored by trade — a higher-beta channel for capital-flow volatility.

insights.claim: The mBridge multi-CBDC platform had handled only 4,047 transactions totaling 387.2 billion yuan as of November 2025, of which 95.3 percent were yuan transactions, against CIPS's roughly 33,000 transactions per day.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: Deflates the digital-yuan-as-dollar-threat thesis with hard numbers; CBDC cross-border rails are immaterial to currency shares today.
insights.quote: as of November 2025, the system had handled 4,047 transactions totaling 387.2 billion yuan, of which 95.3 percent were yuan transactions

insights.claim: Financial Times figures imply mBridge added only about 83 billion yuan of transactions between November 2025 and June 2026 — roughly one-tenth of a single day's average CIPS volume — making it a rounding error in the yuan's international footprint.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete scale benchmark to dismiss mBridge headlines; any claim of CBDC-driven de-dollarization should be checked against one day of CIPS volume.
insights.quote: mBridge volume over the past six to seven months would only represent one-tenth of one day's average CIPS volumes, making mBridge barely a rounding error in the yuan's international footprint.

insights.claim: Cross-border CBDC payments at scale remain years away because no major economy has fully launched a CBDC that could connect to China's, leaving the digital yuan without a network of counterpart systems.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: Network effects, not Chinese technology, are the binding constraint — watch major-economy CBDC launches, not Chinese pilots, as the real trigger.

insights.so_what: Data on Chinese CBDC volumes is unreliable and press-sourced — discount precise mBridge figures and rely on the order of magnitude instead.

themes.theme: Structural gap vs China's economic weight

insights.claim: The yuan still punches far below China's economic weight and China remains tightly tied up in dollar-based global financial networks, which preserves US strategic leverage over Chinese payments despite a decade of internationalization effort.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: US financial-sanctions capacity against China is intact — a key input for pricing tail risk in China-exposed assets and for assessing escalation scenarios.
insights.quote: The yuan overall still punches far below China's economic weight. Far from ditching the dollar, China is still tightly tied up in dollar-based global financial networks.
insights.locator: Conclusion

insights.claim: China's pursuit of yuan internationalization is explicitly motivated by reducing the strategic leverage that ubiquitous dollar payments give the United States, framing currency policy as national security rather than economic efficiency.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: Means Beijing will keep funding uneconomic payment infrastructure regardless of adoption returns — persistent policy tailwind for CIPS buildout irrespective of volumes.
insights.locator: China has long aimed to make the yuan a more important global currency

insights.claim: Even the genuine bright spots in yuan usage — CIPS all-time highs and rising trade settlement — are insufficient for the yuan to keep gaining share of global payments or even of China's own payments.
insights.speaker: Martin Chorzempa
insights.so_what: Bullish yuan datapoints exist but do not aggregate to a trend; require share-based confirmation across SWIFT, CHATS and SAFE before treating any single print as a turn.
insights.quote: However, the bright spots are not enough for the yuan to continue gaining on the dollar in its share of global payments or even overall Chinese payments.
